---
title: "Quiz: cross-correlation with the FFT"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The cross-correlation is $c(t) = \sum_x A(x+t)\,B(x)$; its spectrum is $A_k\overline{B_k}$.

---

**Q1.** Name the three steps that compute the cross-correlation of two images for every shift at once.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two transforms in, one out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
FFT of A and FFT of B; multiply, frequency by frequency, $A_k$ by the complex conjugate of $B_k$; inverse FFT of the product. The result holds $c(t)$ for every shift $t$.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does the conjugate appear? What would you get with $A_k B_k$ instead?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Correlation vs convolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A_kB_k$ is the spectrum of the **convolution** of A and B, which flips B. Correlation does not flip, so B must be flipped once more to undo it; for a real image, flipping in space conjugates the spectrum. With $A_kB_k$ you would compare A with B read backwards.
:::

---

**Q3.** Two signals of 4 samples give $A_k\overline{B_k} = (9, -5i, -1, 5i)$. Which value of the correlation $c(t)$ does $k = 0$ alone contribute to every $t$, and what does it mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The inverse DFT divides by $N = 4$; frequency 0 is the constant wave.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$9/4 = 2.25$ at every shift: the product of the sums of A and B divided by $N$. It says "both images are bright on average", not where they match. That is why the means are usually subtracted first: the constant wave adds the same amount to every shift (circular) or a triangle that grows with the overlap (linear).
:::

---

**Q4.** The FFT gives the **circular** correlation. What does that mean for two tiles that only partly overlap, and how do you get the linear correlation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to the part of B that is pushed out on the right?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The FFT treats both tiles as periodic: what is pushed out on one side comes back on the other, so the score also compares pixels that never lie on top of each other, and a shift $t$ cannot be told from $t - N$. Zero-pad both to at least $2N - 1$ (in practice $2N$) samples per side: the shifted part then falls on zeros, and the result is the linear correlation.
:::

---

**Q5.** Roughly how many times fewer operations does the FFT route need than brute force for two $1024 \times 1024$ tiles, every shift allowed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Brute force: $2N^4$ operations; FFT: three FFTs of $M = 2048^2$ samples at $5M\log_2M$ each.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Brute force $\approx 2.2 \cdot 10^{12}$ operations, the FFT route $\approx 1.4 \cdot 10^9$: about 1600 times fewer.
:::

---

**Q6.** The stage is known to be accurate to $\pm 5$ pixels. Is the FFT still the better choice for a pair of $1024 \times 1024$ tiles?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A window of $\pm w$ costs about $2(2w+1)^2N^2$ operations for $N \times N$ images.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily: $\pm 5$ pixels is $11^2 = 121$ shifts of about $10^6$ pixels, about $2.5 \cdot 10^8$ operations, less than the $1.4 \cdot 10^9$ of the padded FFT route. Brute force over a small window wins up to about $\pm 12$ pixels. The FFT wins when the shift is unknown or large.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that if $g(x) = f(x + t_0)$ (circularly), then $F_k\overline{G_k} = |F_k|^2 e^{-2\pi i k t_0/N}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The shift theorem of the Fourier unit.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$G_k = \sum_x f(x+t_0)e^{-2\pi i kx/N} = e^{2\pi i kt_0/N}\sum_u f(u)e^{-2\pi i ku/N} = e^{2\pi i kt_0/N}F_k$ (with $u = x + t_0$). So $\overline{G_k} = e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N}\overline{F_k}$ and $F_k\overline{G_k} = |F_k|^2e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N}$: the size of each wave squared, with a phase that turns at a rate set by the shift.
:::

---

**Q8.** How can NCC, which divides by the spread of the overlap at every shift, be computed with FFTs?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What sums does NCC need, and how is "the sum of A under B" a correlation?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
NCC needs, at every shift, the sum of products of the overlap, the sums of A and B and the sums of their squares over the overlap. The sum of products is the cross-correlation; the sum of A under B is A correlated with a block of ones the shape of B (a box filter); likewise for $A^2$, B and $B^2$. Each is one product of FFTs; NCC then follows pixel by pixel.
:::
